title: How enzymes work; Factors affecting enzyme activity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EZ01a#t1 term and clue written for the game; EZ02#t2 term and clue written for the game; EZ01a#t3 term and clue written for the game; EZ01a#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EZ01a#N.2b, EZ02#N.3b, EZ01a#N.11, EZ02#N.6b, EZ02#N.14b.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Active site
items.clue: Small pocket or groove on an enzyme where the substrate binds.

items.label: Kinetic energy
items.clue: What molecules gain when warmed, so they move faster and collide more often.

items.label: Metabolism
items.clue: All the chemical reactions in an organism, forming a network of linked pathways.

items.label: Specificity
items.clue: Property by which each enzyme acts on one reaction, or on a few very similar ones.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of an enzyme in a chemical reaction in a cell?

options.text: It speeds up the reaction by joining with the substrate to become the product.
It speeds up the reaction and is left unchanged after the reaction is over.
It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all without it.
It speeds up the reaction by increasing the amount of energy that the reaction releases.

questions.explanation: An enzyme is a catalyst: it increases the rate by lowering the activation energy, and it is not used up. The same enzyme molecule can catalyse the reaction again.

questions.stem: Catalase was added to hydrogen peroxide and the volume of oxygen collected was recorded: 0 s, 0 mL; 20 s, 12 mL; 40 s, 20 mL; 60 s, 24 mL (illustrative data). What is the best estimate of the initial rate of reaction from these data?

options.text: 0.4 mL/s
20 seconds
0.050 per second

questions.explanation: 12 mL of oxygen in the first 20 s gives 12 ÷ 20 = 0.60 mL/s, the best estimate the data allow.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical bacterium, enzyme E catalyses the conversion of compound A to compound B. The conversion of A to B releases energy. A mutation stops the bacterium from making enzyme E. No other enzyme in the bacterium acts on compound A. Which prediction about compound B in the mutant bacterium is best supported?

options.text: B no longer forms at all, as A cannot change into B without enzyme E.
B forms at the normal rate, as the bacterium makes a new enzyme because it needs B.
B forms at the normal rate, as ATP supplies the energy that enzyme E used to supply.
B still forms, but far more slowly, as the reaction is no longer catalysed.

questions.stem: A hypothetical enzyme has its highest rate of reaction at 40 °C. At 45 °C, its rate is lower. Which statement best explains the lower rate at 45 °C?

options.text: Enzyme and substrate molecules move so fast that they pass each other before they are able to bind.
Some hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's shape are disrupted, so the active site fits less well.
Some peptide bonds between the enzyme's amino acids break, splitting its chain into pieces.
Some of the enzyme molecules have been killed by the heat, so fewer are left alive to react.

questions.stem: A hypothetical bacterium makes an enzyme that loses its activity when heated to 50 °C. A student claims that the denaturation of this enzyme at 50 °C is reversible. Which observation, if made, would best support the student's claim?

options.text: Enzyme kept at 50 °C, then returned to 25 °C, regains much of its activity.
Enzyme cooled to 5 °C loses activity and regains it when warmed to 25 °C.
Enzyme heated to 50 °C splits into amino acids, which rejoin into enzyme on cooling.
Bacteria heated to 50 °C survive and then resume growing after being cooled to 25 °C.

questions.explanation: Reversible denaturation means the enzyme regains activity when the condition that disrupted its shape is removed. Activity returning after cooling shows its chain has refolded.
